---
title: "Conditioning: The World After a Clue"
---

Two fair dice have been rolled behind a screen. Someone tells us the first die is two.

The dice have already landed. The clue changes the possibilities relevant to our reasoning.

## 🔰 Retain compatible outcomes {#sec-sample-conditioning-retain-compatible-outcomes}

Before the clue, the model contains 36 equally likely ordered pairs.

The event $B=\{D_1=2\}$ retains just

$$
(2,1),\ (2,2),\ (2,3),\ (2,4),\ (2,5),\ (2,6).
$$

Those pairs carried total probability $6/36=1/6$. Conditioning treats that surviving mass as the new whole.

Each retained pair therefore receives conditional probability

$$
\frac{1/36}{1/6}=\frac16.
$$

The sum is now uniform on $\{3,4,5,6,7,8\}$, even though its original profile was triangular.

## 🏵 The denominator identifies the new whole {#sec-sample-conditioning-the-denominator-identifies-the-new-whole}

For an event $B$ of positive probability,

$$
\mathbb P(A\mid B)
=
\frac{\mathbb P(A\cap B)}{\mathbb P(B)}.
$$

The numerator keeps outcomes compatible with both $A$ and $B$. The denominator measures everything compatible with the clue.

With $A=\{D_1+D_2=7\}$ and $B=\{D_1=2\}$, only $(2,5)$ belongs to the intersection. We obtain conditional probability $(1/36)/(1/6)=1/6$.

The formula needs $\mathbb P(B)>0$. Conditioning a continuous model on an exact real value requires a more careful construction than dividing two zero event probabilities. Interval clues already work with the rule above.

## ⚙️ A probability mask performs the same construction {#sec-sample-conditioning-a-probability-mask-performs-the-same-construction}

For a discrete outcome space, let $W_B[f]$ be one when $f$ belongs to $B$ and zero otherwise. Then

$$
p_B[f]
=
\frac{W_B[f]p[f]}{\sum_gW_B[g]p[g]}.
$$

This is the mask-and-normalize operation on possibilities. It parallels the weighted reduction of observed values, while acting on a different domain.

The selected event has become the reference against which all surviving weights are read.

## 💡 Learning and changing the mechanism are different actions {#sec-sample-conditioning-learning-and-changing-the-mechanism-are-different-actions}

Learning the first die was two does not reroll the second die.

Removing a drawn card from a deck physically changes the source's inventory. Learning which card was removed also changes our knowledge of that inventory.

A model can contain both actions. Keeping them separate prevents an inference rule from silently becoming a claim about intervention or cause.

## ☯ Independence means a clue leaves a law unchanged {#sec-sample-conditioning-independence-means-a-clue-leaves-a-law-unchanged}

For the independent dice,

$$
\mathbb P(D_2=6\mid D_1=2)=\mathbb P(D_2=6)=\frac16.
$$

For repeated draws from a six-card deck without replacement,

$$
\mathbb P(\text{second is six}\mid\text{first is six})=0.
$$

The clue leaves the second die's law unchanged under the model, while revealing a restriction on the deck's next output.

[Bayes](bayes.qmd) uses this same joint description to turn a statement about evidence given a hypothesis into a statement about the hypothesis given the evidence.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try the idea {#sec-sample-conditioning-try-the-idea}

A fair die is known to show an even face. What is the conditional probability that it exceeds three? Identify the new whole before calculating.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Work it through {#sec-sample-conditioning-work-it-through}

The new whole is $\{2,4,6\}$. The desired event retains $\{4,6\}$, giving probability $2/3$. Using all six faces in the denominator would ignore the clue.
:::
